title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that measured validator‑acceptance parity between two NetOps orchestration architectures under shared_initial_candidate semantics: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run used gpt‑5‑mini for generation, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks, and a single shared LLM candidate per paired task (one shared generation per pair). Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120. Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates and do not test independent generator variance or repair efficacy. We provide artifact‑grounded evidence (execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces), an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a nearest‑work comparison matrix, and preregistered protocol modifications required to produce a discriminating independent‑generator head‑to‑head comparison.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require deterministic correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, no transient safety violations) while supporting diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two contrasting architectures are common in research and engineering practice. Translation‑first architectures constrain generation via a vendor‑aware DSL and apply formal verification/solver steps to ensure device guarantees. Agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines centralize generation in a single LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repair or rollback to recover from unsafe or hallucinated proposals.

This study asked a narrowly defined, preregistered confirmatory question chosen after a fresh literature review: for intent‑driven network changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies, which architecture yields higher end‑to‑end operational correctness when measured as deterministic validator acceptance? The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed a paired design (N = 120 paired tasks), declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini and validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and specified shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: a single LLM candidate is generated once per pair and provided identically to both pipeline arms. This design intentionally isolates downstream validator behavior (validator‑acceptance parity) rather than generator variance or independent repair coverage.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment executed under the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter documenting deterministic validator outcomes on 120 paired NetOps intents; (2) an explicit, artifact‑grounded evidence‑to‑claim mapping that states which preregistered hypotheses were actually tested under the shared‑candidate semantics and which remained unobserved; (3) a compact nearest‑work comparison matrix situating these results relative to representative translation→verify and LLM‑agent NetOps studies; (4) precise, preregistered protocol modifications (and the execution artifacts that would change when they are enacted) required to discriminate architectures on independent generator and repair performance.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions frame our positioning. Formal translation→verification and synthesis work emphasize constrained generation and solver‑backed guarantees (e.g., SymNet, "Don't Mind the Gap" and later Weighted NetKAT approaches) where sound device properties are central [10,11,5]. LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research highlights flexible generation, chain‑of‑tool orchestration, and iterative repair; such work stresses deterministic validators to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals (e.g., INTA 2025; IFIP/Networking self‑correcting multi‑agent verifier pipelines) [3,4].

Nearest‑work comparison (compact). We compare four experimental axes: independent generation sampling, repair loop instrumentation, validator‑acceptance focus, and emulator/hardware realism:
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: independent LLM sampling (yes); limited repair loops; partial validator acceptance emphasis; emulator experiments.
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: multi‑agent self‑correcting verifier pipeline (yes generation sampling; yes repair loops; validator acceptance emphasized; Kubernetes policy domain).
• Weighted NetKAT & formal verification literature [5,10–12]: solver‑based synthesis and formal guarantees (independent generation not applicable; solver repairs used; validator acceptance core; verification model domain).
• Present run: shared_initial_candidate semantics (no independent generation sampling), repair_applied = 0 observed (repair instrumentation present but unused), explicit validator‑acceptance focus, Mininet‑derived emulator and synthetic task corpus.

This compact matrix clarifies that the present run provides a precise validator‑acceptance parity measurement under shared candidates and does not replicate independent‑generator comparisons in prior LLM‑sampling experiments.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed the primary estimand as the paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness (A − B) over N_confirmatory = 120 paired tasks, with paired_binary_analysis_v1 as the analysis executor (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar test). Model_scope declared gpt‑5‑mini and the validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 v5.0. The preregistration also froze shared_initial_candidate semantics and a maximum of one repair iteration.

Execution contract and shared_candidate semantics. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter implemented shared_initial_candidate: one LLM generation per paired task was produced and supplied identically to both the translation‑first and agentic orchestration arms. Practical consequences are visible in execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Provider audit metadata in deterministic_reconciliation.json documents hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false (execution isolation holds as preregistered).

Task generation, validator rules, and scoring. Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each manifest entry contains intent, initial and expected final states, required safe sequences, difficulty metadata, and a canonical reference answer (representative entries archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The validator deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and a boolean validation_after.valid. A task passes end‑to‑end correctness only when validation_after.valid == true. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flags, and serve as canonical evidence.

Analysis specifications. Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 as preregistered: compute contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference A − B, bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729), and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Secondary estimands (repair coverage and mean repair iterations) and multiplicity handling (Benjamini–Hochberg for subgroup tests) were preregistered and are reported when observed. All analysis inputs, seeds, and executor settings are archived.

Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 120 and provider audit counts consistent with a single shared generation stage per pair.

Marginal success rates are baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The primary estimand (A − B) = 0.00. Repair and secondary outcomes. Aggregated repair_applied count = 0 for all 240 episodes (execution/scoring/*.json show repair_applied = false per episode); hence preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage are unobserved for this run. Representative per‑task traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json) show shared_initial_candidate equals the normalized reference modulo ordering, parsed_command_count and required_command_count matching, and validation_after.valid = true.

Contamination and missingness. Preregistered contamination checks reported no flags: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty; analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 120 and zero failures. Provider audit metadata shows cache_miss_count = 120 and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, supporting execution isolation and adherence to contamination_plan.

Evidence‑to‑claim mapping (compact, artifact‑grounded). We map preregistered hypotheses to collected evidence and verdicts:
• H1 (Paired difference A − B in end‑to‑end correctness): Measured estimand in this execution = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Supporting artifacts: preregistration (preregistration_sha256 recorded in execution manifest), execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (n11=120,n10=0,n01=0,n00=0), analysis/condition_summary.csv. Verdict: Tested — measured estimand = validator‑acceptance parity; not a test of independent generator or repair robustness.
• H2 (Agentic pipeline higher repair coverage): Supporting artifacts show repair_applied = false across execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Verdict: Unobserved — repair coverage hypothesis could not be evaluated because no repairs were applied in any episode.

Representative example. Pair‑000001 exhibits the typical pattern: shared candidate text equals the canonical reference modulo normalization; execution/scoring/task‑000001‑baseline.json documents parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, normalized_configuration, and validation_after.valid = true (repair_applied = false). Similar representative artifacts for additional pairs are archived in execution/responses/* and execution/scoring/*.
sections.discussion:
What was measured and interpretive boundaries. By design, the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics remove generator variance and make the confirmatory estimand narrowly measure whether downstream orchestration and validators accept identical candidates. The observed degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) therefore demonstrates validator‑acceptance parity: for these synthetic tasks and shared candidates, both pipelines' validators accepted every candidate. This result does not indicate that the architectures would produce identical success rates when each is given independent LLM generations or when repair loops actively alter candidates; those dimensions were outside the measured estimand.

Why repairs were unobserved. The archived per‑task traces and generator metadata indicate that the deterministic synthetic task generator produced candidates that met the validators' full_intent_constraint_validation criteria (normalized command sets matched required sequences). Consequently, repair_applied remained false for all episodes. This factual observation is artifact‑grounded (execution/scoring/*.json) and explains why secondary repair estimands (H2) are unobserved.

Operational implications and follow‑on protocol changes. The run documents a reproducible validator regression and equivalence test useful for validator calibration and orchestrator regression testing. To contrast architectures on independent generator and repair performance the preregistered protocol must be modified in specific, artifact‑verifiable ways (each change will be visible in the execution manifest): (1) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent initial generation (model_calls_used would rise from 120 to 240 for initial candidates); (2) enable multiple sampled generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further increases model_calls); (3) allow and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied > 0 can be observed; (4) increase fidelity (hardware or higher‑fidelity emulator) to reduce simulator‑to‑hardware contamination risk noted in the contamination_plan. These changes are concrete, preregisterable, and their manifestations (model_calls_used, hosted_model_call_event_count, nonzero repair_applied flags) are already defined by the execution contract and will be deterministically recorded.

Threats to validity (condensed). Internal validity: the shared_candidate choice reduces internal variance but narrows the estimand; this was preregistered and executed as declared. Construct validity: deterministic validator acceptance operationalizes correctness per rule set but excludes qualitative operator properties (explainability, maintainability). External validity: synthetic tasks and Mininet‑derived emulation limit generalization to production hardware; single LLM and single validator preclude multi‑model generality. Conclusion validity: degenerate concordance produces point‑mass bootstrap CIs and McNemar p = 1.0 — correct descriptors of observed data but not evidence of equivalence under independent sampling.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair NetOps pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks both validators accepted the identical LLM candidates in every pair (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), producing paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied; preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage remain unobserved. The run therefore demonstrates how shared‑candidate preregistered experiments precisely measure validator‑acceptance parity and provides an artifactized protocol and explicit, verifiable instructions (and manifest signatures) for follow‑ups that would discriminate independent generator and repair performance. All artifacts supporting these claims (preregistration, execution and analysis manifests, per‑task validator traces, and model/adapter declarations) are archived and referenced in the execution manifest included with this submission.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
